content: National lymphatic filariasis morbidity management and disability prevention (LF MMDP) programs should establish monitoring systems tailored to the implementation and outcomes of specific activities under their program's direction. These indicators will vary depending on the scope and design of the MMDP programs in each country. Examples of such indicators include the total number of health workers trained in lymphedema management, the number of health facilities with at least one trained provider in managing lymphedema and acute attacks, and the percentage of health facilities with surgeons trained in hydrocelectomy. Additional indicators might include the number of health education materials displayed in communities to inform patients about the availability of LF services. National programs may also choose to measure the outcomes of their MMDP activities, such as changes in knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors among patients, surgeons, health facility workers, and community members regarding lymphatic filariasis (LF). At the patient level, indicators can include physical, psychosocial, functional, and economic measures. For instance, the frequency of acute attacks is associated with the clinical progression of the disease and serves as a simple and useful proxy for quality of life. Other patient-level indicators might include changes in mobility, standing, walking, or the reported number of workdays lost in the past month. Programs could also assess their success based on improvements in patients' quality of life (QoL). It is important to note that clinical indicators at the patient level do not always reflect the quality of the program, as clinical improvement in lymphedema often depends on patient adherence to recommended management strategies. Therefore, programs are encouraged to use indicators that are within their control. For hydrocele management, indicators such as post-operative hematoma, post-operative hemorrhage, surgical site infection, and recurrence of hydrocele can be used to track program quality. Evaluation of LF programs involves periodic assessments of changes in outcomes, which require technical and financial resources. One measure of program success is the availability and accessibility of facilities staffed with trained health and community workers for managing patients with acute dermatolymphangioadenitis (ADL), lymphedema (or elephantiasis), and hydrocele. The presence of multiple facilities capable of supporting patients with various forms of filariasis, along with flexible care models, indicates successful program expansion and acceptance. Integration of care for other conditions, such as diabetes, leprosy, podoconiosis, and vascular insufficiency, would also serve as a valuable evaluation parameter for national programs. At the patient level, the Dreyer seven-stage classification system for lymphedema provides a detailed framework for assessing disease progression. The stages range from reversible swelling (Stage 1) to the most advanced stage (Stage 7), where patients are unable to perform daily activities independently. Simplified staging for community-level health workers categorizes lymphedema as mild, moderate, or severe, based on the presence of skin changes, folds, or mossy lesions. This simplified system aligns with the seven-stage classification and facilitates community-based management and monitoring.
